Texas Band of Yaqui Indians

The Texas Band of Yaqui Indians, also using Yaqui Nation of Texas, publishes its own account of community identity, family connections and cultural work. This guide places that voice beside a 2015 Texas Senate resolution. It is a starting route into the community’s published perspective, with migration, descent and legal-status questions kept separate.

The complete downloaded 4752×3168 frame and the identification/license/EXIF sections were inspected. This is a modern river landscape, not a photograph of Texas Band members or proof of Indigenous territorial boundaries. It does not identify the cattle as belonging to Yaqui people. These are selected starting points. The full annotated collection, source perspectives, inspection limits and remaining research questions follow below. A starting guide is not an exhaustive history or community endorsement.

01

The community’s own account

The publisher describes connections with Yaqui communities in Sonora and uses Texas Band of Yaqui Indians and Yaqui Nation of Texas for the same community. Its mission emphasizes reconnecting families with heritage, educational opportunities and support for future generations. These self-descriptions provide a community perspective; they do not by themselves independently verify every historical or institutional claim.

Read the sources [1] Texas Band of Yaqui Indians [3] Texas Band of Yaqui Indians

02

What the 2015 resolution records

Senate Resolution989 names and honors the Texas Band, and records adoption on May27,2015. Its historical recitals are the resolution’s statements. A commemorative legislative text should not be used alone to establish genealogical descent, federal recognition, jurisdiction or the details of migration. The original named source remains available so readers can examine what was actually said.

Read the sources [2] Texas Senate

03

Cultural work and a carefully scoped landscape

The mission describes networking, educational and arts-related aims. The credited Yaqui River photograph illustrates Sonora homeland context discussed by the publisher; it does not show Texas Band members, Texas community land or proof of descent. The broader Yaqui guide offers additional historical and language reading, while the Pascua Yaqui Tribe in Arizona remains a distinct government route.

Our Mission — cultural reconnection and community programs ↗

The publisher describes cultural reconnection, family networks, learning and community initiatives. These are its stated purposes and account of its work; they are not independent findings about participation, descent, recognition or outcomes.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Actual public mission body, web lines25–35, and the public arts/networking descriptions at84–110. Institutional/legal-status assertions at38–42 were encountered but not adopted as legal findings. Images, artist works, linked books, member records and underlying genealogies not inspected or reproduced.
